Journal of Shipping and Trade (2026) 11:1 Page 2 of 16 The introduction of the Automatic Identification System (AIS) marked a step forward, as it allows the tracking of the position and destination of a ship. However, it does not provide any data about the route or the estimated time of arrival. In the context of the maritime industry, the Virtual Arrival (VA) policy was initiated by the International Association of Independent Tanker Owners (INTERTANKO) and the Oil Companies International Marine Forum (OCIMF) and aims at reducing emissions and bunkering expenses by slowing down the vessel when there is port congestion. This optimization approach ensures that the ship arrives ‘Just-in-Time’ when a berth and the nautical ser- vices become available, unlike the prevailing first-come first-served practice. In tramp shipping, ship operators tend to “rush to wait” in weak market conditions to take advan- tage of higher demurrage rates compared to freight rates (Adland and Jia 2018). This behaviour can result in port congestion, as well as in higher fuel consumption and ship emissions. The implementation of JIT systems and VA policies can reduce the fuel consump- tion and the environmental footprint of ships. The optimization of sailing speeds for JIT arrival translates into potentially lower average speeds and shorter port waiting times. The information about the slot availability should be provided by the port authority of the discharge port while the vessel is underway or prior to its departure. Therefore, the effectiveness of this operational process depends on transparent communication between vessels and port authorities, existence of reliable technology for speed and route optimization, and collaboration among all stakeholders involved, such as ship operators, charterers, and port authorities. The role of shipbrokers could also be critical (Tsioumas et al. 2023). Despite the benefits of JIT policies, the main barrier to implementing it on a larger scale is the lack of reliable and accurate information about the potential costs and sav- ings (Rehmatulla and Smith 2015). Indeed, JIT solutions are not easy to implement at scale (Sung et al., 2022). The current reality in maritime transportation is that not all stakeholders are willing to promptly adopt JIT, revealing a lack of transparency and wide recognition of this operational practice (Nguyen et al. 2023). Motivated by this gap and considering that the impact of reduced port congestion on the supply side of ships is often overlooked, this study aims to provide a comprehensive assessment of how shorter waiting times in ports (occurring from JIT arrivals) affect the level of freight rates in the dry bulk market. Therefore, the following research question is formulated: What is the impact of reduced port congestion—resulting from speed optimization due to JIT arriv- als—on the freight rates of Capesize bulk carriers? This relationship is examined using time series data and a non-parametric modelling framework. A Random Forest model is developed to simulate the effect of JIT arrivals on Capesize freight rates under various scenarios. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Sect. "Literature review" reviews the relevant literature, Sect. "Data and methodology" outlines the data and methodology, Sect. "Results" presents and analyses the results, and Sect. Journal of Shipping and Trade (2026) 11:1 Page 3 of 16 Literature review The JIT philosophy was initiated in Japan during 1950s and gained increasing popularity when Toyota successfully implemented it in its automotive production system (Monden 2011). JIT is based on the elimination of waste, continuous improvement, and pull pro- duction (Shingo 1989; Hitomi 2017). At the same time, the domain of supply chain man- agement offers fertile ground for the application of JIT principles. The effective application of JIT relies heavily on appropriate coordination among all actors of the supply chain to ensure on-time delivery of the right number of raw mate- rials (Fullerton et al. 2003). The goal is to achieve effective and efficient flow along all supply chain stages and improve responsiveness to customer demands. This highlights the high reliance of JIT supply chains on transportation systems (Morash and Clinton 1997). The weaknesses of shipping and port operations, especially the delays, create bot- tlenecks that are often the reasons for the preference for alternative modes of transport. In this context, maritime and port logistics can benefit from the JIT philosophy if it is adapted to the special characteristics of this business. Mubder (2024) posits that a JIT arrival system, enabled by a Pre-booking Berth Allocation Policy, should synchronize the arrival time of ships with the operating times of cargo handling systems in the port. This is expected to minimize port waiting times, offering cost advantages while improving the port connectivity with the hinterland. Lind et al. (2021) state that JIT should be com- bined with time slots for berthing and data sharing to achieve optimal outcomes. JIT has been presented as a redeeming philosophy for many industries and countries, many times seen as the missing link for industries to return to their base, as with the cost benefits JIT brings, cost minimization might not have to be sought after elsewhere (Shobe 1986). The benefits gained from the streamlining of the supply chain, includ- ing reducing delivery times, as well as the variability in delivery times (Hoffman 2019) and the minimization of wasteful inventory can spill over to the whole value-creation process (Boyd et al. 2002). JIT is a relevant concept with many pertinent applications, especially for transportation and logistics (Goddard 1987; Son 2019; Suwan-Achariya and Sa-Ngobsuk 2012). Logistics and supply chains can benefit from JIT as stemming from mode-choice (Benjamin 1990), cycle optimization (Yu 2012), operator productivity (Sutanto et al. 2019), optimization of production schedules (Bolan 2001), buyer–supplier linkages (Kim and Ha 2003), seasonal demand (Chang and Chou 2013) and/or connec- tivity with Material Requirements Planning (MRP) systems (Park et al. 2017). Yet the JIT philosophy has indeed crept into maritime affairs from many standpoints. Shipping inefficiencies have been mitigated through JIT and STM, based on stakeholder collaboration with the objectives to help reduce (by 15–23%) fuel consumption and Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions (Arjona Aroca et al. 2020). Specifically for ports, the concept of JIT can be of high importance, as traditionally a port is a place of interchange between modes, where some degree of delay is to be expected. This is not due to inher- ent inefficiencies of shipping, but due to the imposed discontinuity of trade flows and differences in scales of the transportation system. These inefficiencies stand contrary to modern ideas with reference to door-to-door transportation and the continuum of the hinterlands and the forelands. Thereby, JIT is a prerequisite for port efficiency and streamlining of the core aspect of ports as transportation terminals—that of being a buffer—with the complex task of attaining the reconciliation of vessel/vehicle capacity and frequency, a daunting task for ports, as they are called upon to seamlessly transfer Tsioumas et al. Journal of Shipping and Trade (2026) 11:1 Page 4 of 16 cargo between and among the very extremes of transportation. Given the high reliance of supply chains on port efficiency, its assessment and improvement have been recurring themes in maritime research (Zahran et al. 2017; Krmac et al., 2023; Zahran et al. 2020; Zhang et al. 2024a, b). In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) has emerged as a promis- ing tool for addressing various aspects of port efficiency (Jahangard et al. 2025). As mentioned, the main benefits of JIT and related policies are the reduction of fuel expenses and greenhouse gas emissions, respectively. While there is extensive research on the latter (Du et al. 2015; GEF-UNDP-IMO GloMEEP Project & GIA, 2020), the present study focuses on the economic aspect. The findings of the IMO-Norway Green- Voyage2050 Global Industry Alliance’s (2020) study indicate that the implementation of JIT arrivals in containerships can reduce fuel consumption by 14.16%, under the sce- nario of speed optimization for the entire voyage. These results complement the MON- ALISA project (2010-EU-21109-S), which suggested potential fuel savings of 10–12%. The research of Du et al. (2015) shows that Virtual Arrival policies entail economic and environmental benefits for both the port and the shipping company. Jia et al. (2017) use AIS data for Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) and offer empirical evidence of the effectiveness of a VA policy in reducing the fuel expenses and emissions. They show that fuel savings range from 7% for a 25% reduction in congestion to 19% when congestion is completely removed. In a more recent study, Tsioumas et al. (2025) find that the imple- mentation of a JIT arrival system in feeder ships may result in a moderate freight rate reduction and enhance the overall competitiveness of Short Sea Shipping (SSS). While estimating the expected impact of JIT arrivals on fuel costs is useful, it does not reflect on the freight rates. Although freight rates are linked to fuel expenses, their formation depends on additional factors (Munim and Schramm, 2017). In this context, this study aims to explore how JIT arrivals may affect freight rates rather than fuel costs or emissions. Many examples and case studies have been put forward, including the use of seamless rail transfer from the vessel (Sáez-Carramolino et al. 2019), vessel arrivals and virtual arrival systems (Senss et al. 2023), and prediction of vessel arrival time and berth allo- cation and quay crane assignment (Yu and Voß 2023). Applications of JIT have indeed been the focus of current research (Panova et al. 2020), many times in conjunction with other relevant and emerging technologies and concepts, such as the electronic data interchange (Annis 1986), mobile interchange structures (Lanzara and D’Ovidio 2000), and traffic and connectivity index forecasts (Panahi et al. 2017). Shipping has been striving to minimize its environmental footprint in recent years, and JIT has been widely acknowledged as a catalyst toward this objective. Indicatively, JIT is utilized in conjunction with green shipping corridors (Fardon 2023), and many times is considered as a distinct item toward transportation sustainability (Røsæg 2019). In addition, JIT is viewed as a precursor of sustainable operations that can minimize the environmental footprint of shipping in specific trades and industries, such as tramp shipping (Merkel et al. 2022), as well as facilitate the efforts of shipping toward carbon intensity mapping (Kim and Eom 2023), emissions’ reduction (Mohammed 2023), digi- talization (Gonzalez et al. 2021), digital twins (Eom et al. 2023), green steaming (Watson et al. 2015), and decarbonation (Stavroulakis et al., 2023). In addition, JIT can be uti- lized for disposal of strategic stocks (Mintiens 1996), timing of estimated times of arrival (Veenstra and Harmelink 2022), optimization of expedited shipping for time-critical Tsioumas et al. Data and methodology Modelling framework and data This study adopts a non-parametric modelling framework for the prediction of the future behaviour of freight rates in response to the implementation of a JIT system on one of the most important routes for the Capesize freight market, i.e. the Tubarao–Qin- gdao iron ore haulage. Given that JIT policies are associated with the optimization of sailing speeds and port congestion, this study aims to offer a quantifiable measure of the impact of such policies on freight rates. A critical tool for this purpose involves a prop- erly specified model that incorporates the key drivers of freight rates. Using this model, we conduct scenario analysis, investigating the percentage change in the freight rates under different scenarios of reduction in the average sailing speed and port congestion. The study of Jia et al. (2017) provides a quantitative assessment of the impact of slower vessel speeds (that result from the implementation of a Virtual Arrival policy) on port waiting time. In our study, we create scenarios where port congestion is reduced by 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. Drawing on the approach of Jia et al. (2017), we estimate the corresponding speed decreases that would result in each of these conges- tion reduction scenarios. The incorporation of the interaction between average speed and port congestion using validated findings, allows for a more accurate representation of their combined impact on freight rates. The scenario analysis of this study is based on the assumption that JIT arrivals imply slower average sailing speeds. It should be noted that there might be cases in which the opposite outcome occurs, and the ship needs to speed up, but this is less likely than the speed reduction (IMO-Norway GreenVoyage2050 Global Industry Alliance 2020). Although we acknowledge these exceptions, we assume that JIT arrivals reduce the aver- age sailing speed across the fleet of Capesize vessels. This is in line with the body of the relevant literature, which primarily treats JIT as a mechanism of downward speed adjustment to avoid unnecessary early arrivals and congestion. The Capesize freight rate of the route under consideration serves as the dependent variable, while the indepen- dent variables capture the supply and demand dynamics. Specifically, the total Chinese iron ore imports are used as a proxy for the demand for Capesize vessels on this route, while the supply side is primarily represented by the Capesize Fleet Development (mea- sured in number of ships). Additionally, the model incorporates the Capesize Average Speed, the Port Congestion Index for Capesize vessels, and the number of idle Cape- sizes. Those three variables reflect the operational efficiency and availability of the fleet and determine the active supply in the short run. Finally, the model includes the Brent Crude Oil Price (1-Month Future). This variable provides a forward-looking perspective that captures market expectations about fuel prices and economic conditions. All data were extracted from Clarksons Research Shipping Intelligence Network and comprise monthly time series from January 2016 to December 2023. The data analy- sis presented in the next section was conducted using Python. Unlike other predictive approaches of freight rates (Tsioumas et al. 2017; Ke et al. 2022), non-parametric models do not assume a specific functional form, offering great flexibility in handling non-lin- ear relationships and dealing with non-stationary time series. Random forest model The Random Forest is a Machine Learning ensemble method introduced by Brei- man (2001), who provided the first theoretical foundation of this type of models. This approach is based on the combined prediction of multiple randomized decision trees for greater accuracy. This supervised learning method is grounded on the “divide and conquer” principle, according to which a randomized tree predictor is grown on small pieces of data fractions, and then the predictors are aggregated by averaging (Biau and Scornet 2016). Random Forests have been used in a variety of applications, including time series fore- casting (Kumar and Thenmozhi 2006; Tyralis and Papacharalampous 2017). Their popu- larity is mainly attributed to their simplicity, flexibility, accuracy, and ability to handle small sample sizes and many variables (Biau and Scornet 2016). Given that the general framework of Random Forests is nonparametric, the variables are not required to be stationary or to satisfy the Classical Linear Regression Model (CLRM) assumptions, such as linear- ity, homoscedasticity, and absence of perfect multicollinearity. The relevant literature provides evidence that most time series in maritime economics (including the variables used in this study) violate several regression assumptions (Kavussanos and Alizadeh-M, 2002; Adland and Cullinane 2006; Tsioumas and Papadimitriou 2018). Therefore, the Random Forest method is well-suited for the nature of the data involved in this study. In addition, this method is highly regarded for its accuracy and effectiveness with small samples, and it can also handle missing data (Breiman, 2003). Random Forests and other Machine Learning methods are increasingly used in vari- ous areas of the maritime sector. Jonquais and Krempl (2019) tested the performance of Machine Learning in predicting the transit time of container shipments, taking into account impactful factors, such as port congestion and seasonality. Similar approaches have demonstrated the effectiveness of Machine Learning (ML) methods for the predic- tion of arrival times of container ships (Nguyen et al. 2024). Wang et al. (2022) applied a Random Forest model for the prediction of the sailing speed of a very large bulk carrier. Saber et al. (2025) provide evidence that the application of an ensemble method can sig- nificantly improve the predictions of Estimated Time of Arrival (ETA) for ships. Recent studies have also employed Machine Learning techniques for the prediction of port con- gestion (Zhang et al. 2024a, b; Ha et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2025), as well as dwell time (Yoon et al. 2023; Chhetri et al. 2025). Relevant studies adopt ML for the prediction of vessel turnaround time (Chu et al. 2024) and decisions tree models and Random Forests for the stay time of ships (Abreu et al. 2023). Random Forests have also been proposed for optimal ship berthing decisions (Han, 2024). Despite their widespread use, the theoretical properties of Random Forests are some- what elusive due to their black-box nature. Denil, Matheson, and De Freitas (2014) address this gap by proving the consistency of a specific regression forest algorithm. They essentially show that the estimators produced by the algorithm converge to an optimal estimator, as the dataset increases to infinity. However, the absence of clear causal inferences offered by regression or vector autoregressive models might be per- ceived as a weakness by some decision-makers. This study addresses this issue through the addition of a scenario-based simulation to offer more intuitive insights. Scenario analysis and cost–benefit analysis The impact of the implementation of a JIT system is assessed by conducting scenario analysis. The Random Forest model can be used for this scenario analysis. We examine the four scenarios presented in Table 4. The change of Capesize rates as a result of a reduction in average speed and port con- gestion highlights the impact of those factors on the formation of freight rates. It is noted that the change of freight rates is expressed relative to the baseline prediction, which is obtained using the mean values of all explanatory variables. A slight reduction of 0.4% in average speed, combined with a modest reduction of 25% in port congestion, is expected to lead to a small decrease of 0.4% in the Capesize voyage freight rate. Scenarios 2, 3, and 4 can lead to a consistent decrease of 11.17% in freight rates. This implies that there is a threshold effect, as the impact on voyage rates stabilizes once port congestion decreases beyond approximately 50%. This indicates that the freight rate reduction is not propor- tional to the operational efficiencies gained, but it is capped at approximately 11%. The economic benefits of virtual arrival policies primarily arise from the reduction in voyage and operating expenses. However, our findings suggest that the implementation of such policies may result in the reduction of potential earnings of ship operators (as the voyage rates are expected to be decreased). The scenario analysis suggests that the implementation of JIT arrivals entails trade-offs for dry bulk operators. For a deeper understanding of the profitability potential arising from JIT, we conduct a conceptual cost–benefit analysis from the per- spective of a dry bulk operator. Table 5 summarizes the key findings. The benefits for operators are not limited to fuel savings (which is perhaps the most significant for them). Given that bulk carriers spend almost 9% of their time waiting at anchorage (IMO-Norway GreenVoyage2050 Global Industry Alliance 2020), the reduc- tion of waiting time can offer operational benefits, such as reduced hull fouling and lower risk of collisions while manoeuvring at anchorage. Also, the predictable arrival time enables better operational planning for maintenance, crew changes, bunkering, and generally improves the asset utilization. In addition, the JIT-induced speed optimiza- tion results in lower emissions, aligning the ship with decarbonization targets. This has financial implications too, as it reduces the exposure of the vessel under consideration to carbon pricing schemes, such as the European Union (EU) Emissions Trading System (ETS). Finally, there are strategic benefits, as the implementation of JIT policies can improve the predictability of ship arrivals, making ship operators more punctual and reliable. This is expected to strengthen the relationship of ship operators with charterers and offer a potential competitive advantage to early adopters. On the cost side, the neces- sary IT support and the associated costs can be a concern for shipping companies. The reduction of freight earnings due to increased short-run supply should also be taken into account, although it is subject to the broad adoption of JIT. Moreover, JIT arrivals reduce the extra demurrage revenue under voyage charters. Lastly, with shorter port waiting times, seafarers have fewer opportunities to spend time ashore. This causes dissatisfac- tion and low morale, which may lead to lower performance and attrition. Therefore, the cost–benefit analysis indicates that the potential profitability of JIT implementation is context-dependent for ship operators. Overall, the results of this study suggest that while the implementation of JIT arrivals generates operational cost savings, it can also reduce freight earnings by increasing the short-run supply of ships. Therefore, the adoption of this practice should not rest on the a priori assumption of positive net profits for bulk carrier operators. In fact, their profit- ability is largely dependent on the magnitude of cost savings achieved, which are criti- cally associated with fuel consumption. Tsioumas et al. Conclusions The relevant literature suggests that JIT operations result in the reduction of average ves- sel speeds and port waiting times. While the direct economic and environmental ben- efits are well documented in the literature, the combined impact of lower sailing speeds and port congestion has not been factored in. This study addresses this gap by conduct- ing scenario analysis within a Random Forest modelling framework. The results suggest that when the implementation of a JIT system leads to a slight decrease in the average sailing speed associated with a 25% drop in port congestion, Capesize freight rates can fall by only 0.4%. A more noticeable reduction of 11.17% is expected if the average speed and port congestion are reduced by 50% and 6.5%, respectively. Overall, it emerges that while lower average speeds and reduced waiting times decrease the expenses of ship operators, their profit margins may not be as high as expected due to the impact of port congestion on the active supply of ships. Shorter waiting times at anchorage increase the availability of the fleet, pushing the freight rates downward. Our findings suggest that this mechanism can cause a reduction in freight rates by up to approximately 11% and no further. The quantification of the expected profit of ship operators requires further research, factoring in the impact of the JIT system implemen- tation on all categories of ship expenses. This study contributes to the literature in several ways. First, it offers empirical evi- dence of the impact of sailing speeds and port congestion on freight rates. Second, it addresses a gap in the economic analysis of JIT implementation in shipping. Finally, it identifies a threshold effect, as the reduction in freight rates stabilizes at a specific level, once port congestion falls beyond a certain point. Therefore, there is an upper limit to freight rate reduction (equal to about 11%). The findings can assist shipowners, charterers, port authorities, and other stakehold- ers in conducting a more comprehensive assessment of the economic impact of JIT sys- tems, taking into account the interaction of all relevant factors. Furthermore, this study suggests that the impact on the active supply can reduce freight rates by up to 11%. This reduction does not necessarily diminish the profitability of ship operators, as it is accom- panied by a decrease in fuel and other operating expenses. Therefore, the net effect on the profitability of bulk carrier operators entails some ambiguity and depends on the relative magnitude of cost savings versus the slight reduction in freight earnings. Beyond the economic perspective, although the earnings potential for operators may need to be revised downward, the lower emissions and improvements in operational efficiency make the wider adoption of JIT systems a pertinent solution for more sustain- able shipping. The broader diffusion of this technology could alleviate port congestion and address a critical bottleneck in maritime supply chains. Tsioumas et al. Journal of Shipping and Trade (2026) 11:1 Page 13 of 16 This study does not aim to disincentivize the adoption of JIT systems, but to provide a more accurate assessment of their economic impact. However, the benefits of JIT arriv- als cannot be realized without a broad and effective implementation of this practice. Policy actions—such as incentives in the form of lower port dues—are important steps during the current transitional phase. At the same time, port authorities should invest in digital platforms that enable real-time data exchange and ensure coordination with all relevant stakeholders. Ship operators, for their part, should not be passive recipients of these systems but should actively integrate JIT into voyage planning and adjust their operational practices in such a way as to maximize the efficiency gains and fully realize the benefits of this technology. JSON: Name: jit_impact_capesize_rf Title: Random forest-based quantification of the impact of JIT-induced sailing speed and port congestion changes on Capesize Tubarao–Qingdao freight rates Short Hypothesis: A coordinated reduction in average sailing speed and port congestion caused by JIT implementation produces a measurable decrease in Capesize Tubarao–Qingdao voyage freight rates. Related Work: Prior work has examined JIT/Virtual Arrival policies and their effects primarily on fuel consumption and emissions, using voyage-level optimization, AIS-based empirical analyses, and berth allocation models. Other strands include econometric and time-series models for freight-rate forecasting and ML-based predictions for ETA, port congestion, and vessel speed. Existing approaches that quantify economic effects either focus on operating-cost reductions (fuel/emissions) or treat freight-rate behavior with linear or parametric econometric models that assume stationarity and fixed functional forms. Machine learning studies address ETA and congestion prediction but rarely integrate freight-rate outcomes with operational variables. Limitations in the literature include: (1) limited joint modelling of sailing speed, port congestion, and supply-side availability when predicting freight rates; (2) reliance on parametric assumptions that are violated by maritime time series; (3) sparse scenario analyses that fail to reveal non-linear or threshold effects; and (4) insufficient ablation studies to measure the relative contribution of operational vs. macro controls to freight-rate dynamics. Abstract: This research pipeline quantifies how just-in-time (JIT) arrival practices affect Capesize voyage freight rates by jointly modelling operational and market drivers using a non-parametric ensemble method. The pipeline employs a Random Forest regression trained on monthly time series of the Tubarao–Qingdao Capesize voyage rate, Capesize average sailing speed, a Capesize port congestion index, fleet development and idle tonnage, demand proxies, and a forward oil-price indicator. The core contribution is a reproducible experimental workflow: (1) time-series-aware model selection and hyperparameter tuning; (2) counterfactual scenario simulations that map congestion reductions to speed adjustments; and (3) comparative and ablation studies against parametric and alternative ML baselines. Expected outcomes are robust estimates of freight-rate sensitivity to JIT-induced operational changes, identification of non-linear or threshold effects in rate responses, and quantified uncertainty bounds for scenario-driven rate projections. The pipeline produces interpretable feature-attribution and scenario reports to inform operators and port authorities on the net economic implications of JIT adoption. Experiments: Datasets: monthly series January 2016–December 2023 from Clarksons Research SIN comprising: (a) Tubarao–Qingdao Capesize voyage freight rate (dependent), (b) Capesize average sailing speed, (c) Capesize Port Congestion Index, (d) Capesize fleet development (number of vessels), (e) idle Capesizes, (f) Chinese iron ore imports (demand proxy), (g) Brent crude oil 1-month future price, and (h) monthly seasonality dummies. Preprocessing: time-order-preserving imputation for missing values, standardization for ML methods where required, and creation of interaction features (speed × congestion). Baselines: ordinary least squares (OLS) with seasonality, vector autoregression (VAR) on differenced stationary transforms, decision tree, support vector regression (SVR), and XGBoost. Model selection: rolling-origin cross-validation with 12-month test folds; hyperparameter tuning via randomized search optimizing validation RMSE. Primary evaluation metrics: R2, MAE, RMSE, and prediction-interval coverage at 90%. Secondary diagnostics: residual autocorrelation (Ljung–Box), prediction calibration, and feature-attribution via permutation importance and SHAP values. Scenario experiments: four counterfactual scenarios mapping congestion reductions of 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% to associated empirically estimated average-speed decreases; generate out-of-sample counterfactual predictions and report percent change vs. baseline with bootstrap 95% CIs (n=1,000). Ablation studies: (A) remove Port Congestion Index, (B) remove average speed, (C) remove supply-side controls (fleet development and idle tonnage), and (D) replace Random Forest with each baseline to quantify contribution to counterfactual effect size and predictive accuracy. Robustness checks: (i) exclude pandemic 2020–2021 months and re-run pipeline, (ii) perform block-bootstrap stability analysis, (iii) test alternative congestion→speed mappings estimated by an auxiliary regression. Statistical tests: paired comparison of predictive errors (Diebold–Mariano) between Random Forest and best baseline; test significance of predicted rate changes via bootstrap-derived CIs. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data quality and measurement error: the Port Congestion Index, speed aggregates, and route-specific rate series may contain construction error, missingness, or heterogeneous reporting. Sample size and nonstationarity: monthly data from 2016–2023 yields a modest number of training points and includes structural breaks (e.g., pandemic), limiting statistical power and extrapolation. Causal identification: the pipeline is predictive/counterfactual and cannot establish causal mechanisms; omitted confounders (charter market frictions, ballast routing choices, modal substitution) may bias inferred effects. Model limitations: Random Forest is a black-box with limited causal interpretability and can misrepresent temporal dependence if not properly cross-validated; feature interactions may be unstable. Scenario mapping uncertainty: converting congestion reductions to fleet-average speed changes relies on auxiliary estimates and literature-derived mappings and introduces model risk. External validity: results calibrated on the Tubarao–Qingdao Capesize corridor may not generalize to other routes, vessel sizes, or liner trades. Economic equilibrium effects: market adjustments (charterer behavior, supply reallocation) beyond the short-run predictive window are not modelled and may alter long-term freight-rate responses. Computational constraints are modest but increased bootstrap and CV budgets raise runtime for reproducibility.
